newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: TENNIS-SPAIN REIGNS AT SWISS OPEN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SPAIN REIGNS AT SWISS OPEN.

text.p: South Africa's Wayne Ferreira alone withstood a Spanish sweep of the quarter-finals at the Swiss Open on Friday as second seed Alex Corretja and two compatriots reached the final four.

Displaying the devastating form which has already earned him two tournament wins this season, Corretja needed just 65 minutes to book his place in the semifinals with a thorough 6-4 6-0 win over seventh-seeded compatriot Alberto Berasategui.

"On a scale of 10, today I think I was a 10," said Corretja, playing in his first event since losing in the fourth round of the French Open to Belgian qualifier Filip Dewulf. "I couldn't have played any better, I made no mistakes.
"My game was really solid, it would have been difficult to beat me today."
Corretja will now meet fellow Spaniard Juan Albert Viloca, who swept aside Germany's Nicolas Kiefer 6-4 6-3 to reach his first semifinal this season.

Viloca, who registered his first victory over a top 10 opponent with a second round win over world number nine Marcelo Rios, will have to clear a tougher hurdle in the form of his sixth-ranked compatriot if he is to reach the first final of his career.
A winner in Estoril and Rome and a finalist on two other occassions, Corretja has been the dominant clay-court player this season, winning 28 matches -- more than any other player.
Sixth seed Felix Mantilla, who lost last year's final to Albert Costa, became the third Spaniard to advance with a 6-4 6-3 win over compatriot Javier Sanchez.
Mantilla, searching for back-to-back tournament wins after his victory in Bologna, will now take on eighth-seeded Ferreira.
The 25-year-old South African, producing what he described as his best tennis in a disappointing year, overcame local favourite Marc Rosset 7-5 7-6 (12-10) to reach his first semifinal this season.

"In this wonderful year I've had, this was probably my best match," said Ferreira, who finished last season ranked 10 in the world but has since slipped to number 26. "I've had reasons for my bad play but none to explain why I've been playing this bad.
"I just had a few little injuries at the start of year, didn't play well and lost confidence."
The only player standing in the way of a sixth Spanish win in seven years, Ferreira believes the high altitude at the Swiss resort and fast clay could aid his cause.
"Playing on clay at this altitude suits my game, I can be more aggressive," Ferreira said. "But all the Spaniards are tough -- even the new ones.
"There are new players every week, I played one here I had never seen before.
"They all play the same, different face -- same player."
